paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יְהוָה֙ אֶל־אַבְרָ֔ם לֶךְ־לְךָ֛ מֵאַרְצְךָ֥ וּמִמּֽוֹלַדְתְּךָ֖ וּמִבֵּ֣ית אָבִ֑יךָ אֶל־הָאָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר אַרְאֶֽךָּ׃

i18n.en: YHWH said to Abram, "Go forth from your land, from your kindred, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter opens the patriarchal narratives with a single verb whose grammar resists single-English rendering.** *Lekh-lekha* — לֶךְ־לְךָ — is the qal imperative of *halakh* ('go') followed by a *lamed*-prefixed second-person pronoun. The construction is the so-called **ethical dative** (or dative of advantage / dative of interest): the *lamed* + pronoun adds a reflexive overtone — *go for yourself*, *go on your own account*, or in the most expansive scholarly reading, *go to your-self* (i.e., into your own becoming). // **Three readings circulate.** (a) The classical philological position treats the *lamed* as redundant intensification — Hebrew imperative idiom occasionally takes a dative pronoun without independent semantic load (cf. *qum-lakh*, *shuv-lakh*). On this reading the standard ASV 'get thee out' captures the sense. (b) Rashi, drawing on rabbinic tradition (Genesis Rabbah 39:9), reads the *lamed* as *l'ha'natah'kha v'l'tovat'kha* — *for your benefit and for your good* — the journey is divinely-prescribed Abrahamic enrichment. (c) The modern critical consensus (Sarna, JPS Torah Commentary, 1989; Alter, *The Five Books of Moses*, 2004; Hamilton, NICOT, 1990) reads the *lamed* as a genuine ethical dative carrying a reflexive-advantageous nuance that resists smoothing — the journey is *for yourself*, the new identity is *toward yourself*. // **The phrase recurs only once more in the Hebrew Bible: Gen 22:2**, the *aqedah*, where YHWH commands Abraham *lekh-lekha el eretz ha-Moriah* — *go forth to the land of Moriah* — to offer Isaac. The doubled use forms a deliberate *inclusio* across the Abraham cycle: the call that opens it (12:1, leave father's house) and the call that closes it (22:2, offer the son who is the future) are marked with the same idiom. Sarna and Alter both emphasize the rhetorical bracket. // The WoH translation reads 'Go forth' — intensified over bare 'go', neutral on the ethical-dative philological question, leaving the inclusio with 22:2 to be marked at that verse. The reflexive-advantageous resonance is left for commentary.

paragraphs.text: וְאֶֽעֶשְׂךָ֙ לְג֣וֹי גָּד֔וֹל וַאֲבָ֣רֶכְךָ֔ וַאֲגַדְּלָ֖ה שְׁמֶ֑ךָ וֶהְיֵ֖ה בְּרָכָֽה׃

i18n.en: I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will make your name great; and you shall be a blessing.

paragraphs.commentary: **The promise has four clauses in escalating scope.** *I will make of you a great nation* — *agadellekha l'goy gadol* — promises numeric and political mass; *I will bless you* — *avarekhekha* — promises personal divine favor; *I will make your name great* — *agadelah shemekha* — promises lasting reputation; *and you shall be a blessing* — *vehyeh berakhah* — turns Abram from recipient to source. The final clause is the structural pivot: the blessing flowing *toward* Abram in the first three clauses now flows *through* him in the fourth, setting up the universal-scope promise of v3. // The phrase *agadelah shemekha* — *I will make your name great* — directly answers and reverses the Babel-builders' *naase lanu shem* of 11:4 (*let us make for ourselves a name*). What humanity tried to seize collectively at Babel through architecture and coordination, YHWH now grants to one individual through covenantal call. The chapter is deliberately staging the contrast: the *shem*-ambition that ended in dispersion (11:8) reappears as the *shem*-promise that opens the covenant-line.

paragraphs.text: וַאֲבָֽרֲכָה֙ מְבָ֣רְכֶ֔יךָ וּמְקַלֶּלְךָ֖ אָאֹ֑ר וְנִבְרְכ֣וּ בְךָ֔ כֹּ֖ל מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת הָאֲדָמָֽה׃

i18n.en: I will bless those who bless you, and the one who curses you I will curse; and in you all the families of the ground shall be blessed.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter's load-bearing verse — the universal-scope promise that makes Genesis 12 the literary opening of the covenant arc.** Two philological questions sit at its center. // **First, the curse-verbs.** The verse uses *two* distinct verbs for cursing in immediate parallel: *m'qallel'kha a'or* — *the one cursing you (qillel) I will curse (arar)*. *Qillel* (from q-l-l, 'be slight, treat as trifling') names a contemptuous diminishment — to *curse* in the sense of *belittle* or *speak slightingly of*. *Arar* (a-r-r) names a stronger juridical curse — the cursing that excludes from blessing-flow (the same root used at 3:14, 3:17, 4:11, 9:25). The verse is not redundant: a mild contempt directed at Abram triggers a juridical exclusion from YHWH. Sarna (JPS, 1989) and Alter (2004) both flag the verb asymmetry; the WoH translation preserves it as 'curse' for both, with the lexical detail surfaced here. // **Second, and more contested: *v'nivrakhu vekha kol mishpechot ha-adamah*.** The verb *nivrakhu* is **niphal** at this verse — passive: *shall be blessed*. But the parallel formulae at Gen 22:18 and 26:4 are pointed **hithpael** — middle / reflexive: *shall bless themselves*. The Masoretic Text itself preserves both forms across the five iterations of the promise: niphal at 12:3, 18:18, 28:14; hithpael at 22:18, 26:4. // **Three positions on what the verse means.** (a) The traditional Christian reading, going back to the LXX *eneulogēthēsontai* and confirmed by Paul's citation in Galatians 3:8 ("in you shall all the nations be blessed"), reads the verb as straightforwardly passive across all five occurrences. The MT pointing at 12:3 (niphal) supports this reading at this verse. (b) The modern critical consensus (Speiser, *Anchor Bible Genesis*, 1964; Sarna, JPS, 1989; Westermann, *Genesis 12–36*, Hermeneia, 1985; NJPS) reads the original idiom as middle/reflexive across all five verses: *by you all the families of the ground shall bless themselves* — i.e., they shall invoke Abram's name as a paradigm of blessing (cf. Gen 48:20, *by you shall Israel bless, saying, 'Elohim make you as Ephraim and Manasseh'*). On this reading the niphal pointings at 12:3 / 18:18 / 28:14 are Masoretic harmonization toward the theologically richer passive sense, against an original consistent hithpael. (c) Wenham (*WBC*, 1994) and Hamilton (*NICOT*, 1990) split the difference, suggesting the niphal/hithpael distinction was meaningful for the redactor and should be preserved verse-by-verse — passive here, middle at 22:18. // **The Pauline reception is decisive for the Christian translation tradition.** Galatians 3:8 quotes the verse as *eneulogēthēsontai en soi panta ta ethnē* — *in you shall all the nations be blessed* — and reads the passive as the textual foundation of the gospel-to-the-gentiles. ASV, RSV, NRSV, and most English translations in the Christian tradition follow Paul. NJPS, the JPS Tanakh, and Alter follow the modern critical reading and render middle. // **The WoH translation reads passive at this verse, matching the MT niphal pointing here.** The choice is local: the passive matches the pointed text at 12:3 specifically, and the middle/reflexive will be the rendering at 22:18 and 26:4 where the MT itself points hithpael. The verse-by-verse approach preserves the MT's own variation rather than smoothing toward either pole. Commentary at 22:18 will mark the seam.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ אַבְרָ֗ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבֶּ֤ר אֵלָיו֙ יְהוָ֔ה וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ אִתּ֖וֹ ל֑וֹט וְאַבְרָ֗ם בֶּן־חָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנִים֙ וְשִׁבְעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה בְּצֵאת֖וֹ מֵחָרָֽן׃

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֣ח אַבְרָם֩ אֶת־שָׂרַ֨י אִשְׁתּ֜וֹ וְאֶת־ל֣וֹט בֶּן־אָחִ֗יו וְאֶת־כָּל־רְכוּשָׁם֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר רָכָ֔שׁוּ וְאֶת־הַנֶּ֖פֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר־עָשׂ֣וּ בְחָרָ֑ן וַיֵּצְא֗וּ לָלֶ֙כֶת֙ אַ֣רְצָה כְּנַ֔עַן וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ אַ֥רְצָה כְּנָֽעַן׃

i18n.en: Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all the substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had made in Haran; and they went out to go to the land of Canaan, and to the land of Canaan they came.

paragraphs.commentary: **The unusual phrase *ha-nefesh asher asu b-Charan* — *the souls that they had made in Haran*** — has no exact idiomatic parallel in the Hebrew Bible. *Asah* (make / do) does not standardly take *nefesh* (soul / person) as object. The verse forces a decision and three readings circulate. // (a) **The proselyte reading** — Rashi (following Sifrei Deuteronomy 32 and Onkelos's targum *de'sha'abidu l'oraita*, 'those whom they made subject to the Torah') reads *asu* as *converted, made into adherents*. On this reading Abram and Sarai conducted a missionary enterprise in Haran and brought converts with them. The reading has deep traditional roots but no philological support outside the rabbinic-targumic tradition. // (b) **The slaves-acquired reading** — Speiser (*Anchor Bible Genesis*, 1964), Sarna (JPS, 1989), and Westermann (*Genesis 12–36*, 1985) read *asu* as a variant of *qanah* (acquire), parallel to the *rekhush asher rakhashu* (substance that they had gathered) of the immediately preceding clause. The *nefesh* here are household slaves and dependents acquired by purchase in Haran. The parallelism with *rekhush rakhashu* is structurally tight. // (c) **The dependents / household reading** — a softer version of (b): the *nefesh* are the broader household — slaves, dependents, attached persons — without specifying the mode of acquisition. NJPS renders 'the persons that they had acquired in Haran'; NRSV 'the persons whom they had acquired in Haran'. // The literal Hebrew *asu* (*made*) is unusual and the WoH translation preserves the oddness as 'the souls that they had made' — matching ASV's 'gotten' in keeping the literal verb, leaving the proselyte/slaves question for the reader. The chapter's later content (vv 16, 20 — male and female slaves listed among Abram's holdings) suggests the household-economy reading is the one the chapter assumes, but the verse-form itself declines to disambiguate.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּעֲבֹ֤ר אַבְרָם֙ בָּאָ֔רֶץ עַ֚ד מְק֣וֹם שְׁכֶ֔ם עַ֖ד אֵל֣וֹן מוֹרֶ֑ה וְהַֽכְּנַעֲנִ֖י אָ֥ז בָּאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: Abram passed through the land to the place of Shechem, to the oak of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land.

paragraphs.commentary: **Abram's first stop in the promised land is a sacred tree at a name-bearing oracle site.** *Elon Moreh* — אֵלוֹן מוֹרֶה — is two lexically loaded words. // **First, *elon*.** The botanical identification is contested in Hebrew lexicography. *Elon* (אֵלוֹן), *elah* (אֵלָה), and *alon* (אַלּוֹן) are three related forms that can refer to *oak*, *terebinth*, or large-tree-of-sacred-significance generally. BDB groups all three under 'oak / terebinth'; HALOT distinguishes *alon* (oak) from *elah/elon* (terebinth) with less than full confidence. The LXX renders δρῦς (oak) here. Modern scholarly translations vary: ASV 'oak', NJPS 'terebinth', NRSV 'oak'. The WoH translation reads 'oak' with ASV — the tree-species precision is not load-bearing for the verse. // **Second, *Moreh*.** The proper-name form derives from the root y-r-h, 'to throw, point, teach, give oracle / *torah*'. *Moreh* is the hiphil participle: *teacher, one who instructs, oracle-giver*. The word retains its semantic transparency throughout the Hebrew Bible — *moreh* appears in Isa 9:14, Isa 30:20, Hab 2:18, Prov 5:13, Job 36:22 as a common noun meaning 'teacher / instructor'. **The 'oak of Moreh' is therefore plausibly read as 'oak of the Teacher / oak of the Oracle-Giver'** — a sacred-tree site associated with prophetic / divinatory consultation. // **The sacred-tree pattern in Genesis and the patriarchal corpus is consistent.** *Elon Moreh* recurs at Deut 11:30 (the blessing-and-curse ceremony on Gerizim and Ebal happens *etzel elonei Moreh*). Jacob buries the foreign gods *under the oak which was at Shechem* (Gen 35:4) — the same place. Deborah is buried *under the oak below Bethel* called *Allon Bakhut* (Gen 35:8). Joshua sets up a stone *under the oak that was by the sanctuary of YHWH* at Shechem (Josh 24:26). Judges 6:11 places the angelic call of Gideon *under the oak which was in Ophrah*. Judges 9:6, 37 names *elon mutzav* and *elon m'on'nim* (the oak of the diviners) at Shechem. // The pattern is unmistakable: trees at Shechem and elsewhere function as theophany-and-oracle sites in the patriarchal and pre-monarchic narratives. The verse here is naming the spot where the first patriarchal theophany (v 7) will immediately follow — and a sacred-tree-oracle context is exactly what the next verse will deliver. // *V'ha-Kena'ani az ba-aretz* — *and the Canaanite was then in the land* — is the chapter's first parenthetical historical aside, marking the temporal seam between the narrative present (Abram's day) and the redactor's later vantage when the Canaanites were no longer 'in the land' as the dominant population. The aside discloses the redactor's perspective without resolving the dating question.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּרָ֤א יְהוָה֙ אֶל־אַבְרָ֔ם וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לְזַ֨רְעֲךָ֔ אֶתֵּ֖ן אֶת־הָאָ֣רֶץ הַזֹּ֑את וַיִּ֤בֶן שָׁם֙ מִזְבֵּ֔חַ לַיהוָ֖ה הַנִּרְאֶ֥ה אֵלָֽיו׃

i18n.en: YHWH appeared to Abram and said, "To your seed I will give this land." And he built there an altar to YHWH who had appeared to him.

paragraphs.commentary: **The first theophany to a patriarch — and the nuclear form of the land-promise that will be elaborated across the patriarchal cycle.** Two glossary-grade items in one verse. // **First, *va-yera YHWH el-Avram*.** The verb is *yera*, the niphal of r-a-h (see), conjugated as 'was seen / appeared / let himself be seen / made himself visible'. The niphal is mediopassive: it can be read as YHWH being passively *seen by* Abram (the receptive sense) or as YHWH actively *causing himself to be seen* (the reflexive-causative sense). The standard English 'appeared' smooths the niphal into a colorless intransitive — *appeared* in English suggests sudden visibility without specifying its mode. The Hebrew preserves the question of whether the seeing originates with the seer or with the seen. // **The theophany-formula *va-yera YHWH* recurs across the patriarchal narratives:** to Abram at 17:1 (the covenant of circumcision), to Abraham at 18:1 (the visit at Mamre — where the appearance is explicitly embodied as three men), to Isaac at 26:2 and 26:24 (Beersheba), to Jacob at 35:9 (return from Paddan-Aram). The formula bookends every major covenantal moment in the Abraham–Isaac–Jacob arc. The chapter is introducing the patriarchal-theophany pattern with this verse; the *mode* of the seeing is left unspecified here and only becomes explicitly embodied at 18:1. // **The chapter does not specify the mode of seeing.** The Wheel of Heaven lens here is measured: chapters 1–11 have established a context in which *elohim* are a plural senior class that interact with humans through embodied descent (the *vayered YHWH* of 11:5 and 11:7) and through audible speech (4:6, 6:13). The first patriarchal theophany at 12:7 fits the same register — a localized presence that becomes visible, speaks, and gives a promise. The chapter does not editorialize. // **Second, *l'zarakha eten et-ha-aretz ha-zot*.** Seven Hebrew words constitute the nuclear form of the land-promise. *Zera* (seed) — the agricultural-biological term for offspring / posterity / line — will be the chapter's recurring designator for Abram's progeny across the patriarchal arc. The promise-formula will be expanded at 13:14–17 (with quadrant directions and innumerable-as-dust imagery), 15:7–21 (with the cut-covenant ritual and the explicit Euphrates-to-the-river-of-Egypt boundaries), 17:8 (as 'an everlasting possession'), 22:17 (with the seashore-sand imagery), 26:3 (to Isaac), 28:13 (to Jacob), and elsewhere. Verse 12:7 is the bare nucleus: *to your seed I will give this land*. // The WoH translation preserves *seed* over the modern smoothings 'offspring' (NIV) and 'descendants' (RSV, NRSV), matching ASV. The agricultural metaphor — seed-in-ground, growth, multiplication — is the patriarchal cycle's load-bearing image and will recur through the chapter and corpus. // **The altar.** *Vayyiven sham mizbeach la-YHWH ha-nire'eh elav* — *he built there an altar to YHWH who had appeared to him*. The altar-building marks the site as a cult-place: the spot of the theophany is now spatially designated. The chapter is establishing the patriarchal pattern of cult-site-foundation, which will continue at Bethel (v 8) and Hebron (13:18). The first patriarchal altar is *under the oak at Shechem* — the sacred-tree-and-altar combination that the later cult would not maintain in the same form.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּעְתֵּ֨ק מִשָּׁ֜ם הָהָ֗רָה מִקֶּ֛דֶם לְבֵֽית־אֵ֖ל וַיֵּ֣ט אָהֳלֹ֑ה בֵּֽית־אֵ֤ל מִיָּם֙ וְהָעַ֣י מִקֶּ֔דֶם וַיִּֽבֶן־שָׁ֤ם מִזְבֵּ֙חַ֙ לַֽיהוָ֔ה וַיִּקְרָ֖א בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְהוָֽה׃

i18n.en: He moved on from there to the hill country east of Bethel and pitched his tent, with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east; and he built there an altar to YHWH and called on the name of YHWH.

paragraphs.commentary: **The second altar in two verses, and the introduction of the *qara b'shem YHWH* formula in the patriarchal corpus.** // *Vayyiqra b'shem YHWH* — *and he called on the name of YHWH* — is one of the Hebrew Bible's stable formulae for **cult-site invocation**. The phrase *qara b'shem YHWH* (literally *call with/in the name of YHWH*) covers a semantic range from worship-invocation through proclamation of the name through ritual naming. The phrase was first introduced at Gen 4:26, in the closing notice of the Seth-Enosh genealogy: *az huchal liqro b'shem YHWH* — *then it was begun to call on the name of YHWH* — marking the antediluvian origin of YHWH-cult. // **The patriarchal recurrences mark altar-sites along the Abrahamic and Isaac itineraries:** here at 12:8 (the hill country between Bethel and Ai); 13:4 (return to the same altar after the descent to Mitsrayim — the chapter is structurally framing the Mitsrayim episode between two callings-on-the-name at Bethel); 21:33 (Abraham at Beersheba, after planting a tamarisk); 26:25 (Isaac at Beersheba). The verb is the patriarchal altar-formula. // The chapter is establishing Abram as the resumption of the Seth-Enosh YHWH-cult tradition — the one whose line had been broken by Babel and the dispersion. The first thing Abram does on entering the promised land is to re-found the worship that had begun at Enosh's generation and been interrupted by the post-Flood human ambition. // The geographic detail *Beth-El miyam v'ha-Ai miqedem* (Bethel on the sea-side, Ai on the east) names the precise topographic position with respect to the two later-important towns. Bethel will be Jacob's theophany site (Gen 28); Ai will be the site of Israel's first conquest setback (Josh 7–8). The chapter is geographically dense with future-narrative resonance.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּסַּ֣ע אַבְרָ֔ם הָל֥וֹךְ וְנָס֖וֹעַ הַנֶּֽגְבָּה׃ (פ)

i18n.en: Abram journeyed on, going and journeying toward the Negev.

paragraphs.commentary: **The doubled infinitive-absolute construction.** *Halokh v'naso'a* — *going and journeying* — pairs two infinitives-absolute to mark *continuous, progressive* motion: 'going on continuously', 'kept journeying'. The Hebrew idiom intensifies what a single verb would say. ASV: 'going on still toward the South'. // The *Negev* (הַנֶּגֶב, *the south / the dry-country*) is the semi-arid southern region of Canaan, between the central hill country and the Sinai. The chapter is positioning Abram in the southern Negev just before the famine of v 10 will push him further south into Egypt — the geographic sequence is Shechem → Bethel/Ai → Negev → Mitsrayim, a steady southward progression that will pivot at Mitsrayim and return.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֥י רָעָ֖ב בָּאָ֑רֶץ וַיֵּ֨רֶד אַבְרָ֤ם מִצְרַ֙יְמָה֙ לָג֣וּר שָׁ֔ם כִּֽי־כָבֵ֥ד הָרָעָ֖ב בָּאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: There was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Mitsrayim to sojourn there, for the famine was heavy in the land.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter pivots into the wife-sister type-scene.** *Vayered Avram Mitsraymah* — *Abram went down to Mitsrayim*. // The verb *yarad* (descend / go down) is the Hebrew Bible's standard geographic register for movement to Egypt. The Levant is topologically *up* relative to the Nile delta — both in elevation (Canaan's hill country is hundreds of meters above sea level; the eastern Delta is at or near sea level) and in Hebrew cardinal-orientation conventions (south is *down*). The verbal pattern *yarad ... Mitsraymah* is consistent across the corpus: Joseph is *brought down* to Egypt (Gen 39:1); Jacob *goes down* to Mitsrayim (Gen 46:3); the credal recapitulation in Deut 26:5 opens with *Arami oved avi vayered Mitsraymah* — *my father was a wandering Aramean, and he went down to Mitsrayim*. The Exodus reverses the descent: Israel *comes up* (*aliyah*) out of Mitsrayim. // The verbal pattern is also a thematic pattern. Going down to Mitsrayim in the patriarchal corpus is structurally the move into peril-with-deliverance: famine drives the descent (here at 12:10, again at 42–47 for Jacob's household), foreign-court complications follow (Pharaoh here, Potiphar's house and the imprisonment for Joseph), and divine intervention restores. The Abram-going-down at 12:10 is the **first instance of a pattern** that will end in the Exodus. // **Robert Alter, *The Art of Biblical Narrative* (1981, expanded 2011), is the canonical scholarly treatment of the wife-sister sequence as a *type-scene*.** Three instances appear in Genesis: 12:10–20 (Abram, Sarai, Pharaoh), 20:1–18 (Abraham, Sarah, Abimelech of Gerar), 26:1–11 (Isaac, Rebekah, Abimelech of Gerar). All three share the same narrative skeleton — patriarch travels to foreign land under duress; pre-empts the danger of foreign king seeing his wife by passing her off as his sister; wife is taken into foreign king's house; YHWH intervenes; king discovers the deception and returns the wife with rebuke. The repetition with variation is the diagnostic feature of biblical type-scene composition. // The classical source-critical reading (Gunkel; Speiser, 1964) treats the three as variant traditions preserved by different sources (12:10–20 = J; 20 = E; 26 = J again). The modern literary-critical reading (Alter; Sternberg, *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative*, 1985) treats them as deliberate narrative repetition — the same scene played three times to develop character, contrast patriarchs, and trace ethical maturation across the cycle. The two readings are not mutually exclusive. // The chapter is here opening the first instance of one of the corpus's most studied type-scenes. The remaining verses (11–20) will play it out.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֕י כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר הִקְרִ֖יב לָב֣וֹא מִצְרָ֑יְמָה וַיֹּ֙אמֶר֙ אֶל־שָׂרַ֣י אִשְׁתּ֔וֹ הִנֵּה־נָ֣א יָדַ֔עְתִּי כִּ֛י אִשָּׁ֥ה יְפַת־מַרְאֶ֖ה אָֽתְּ׃

i18n.en: As he drew near to enter Mitsrayim, he said to Sarai his wife, "Behold now, I know that you are a woman beautiful of appearance.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Ishah yefat-mar'eh*** — אִשָּׁה יְפַת־מַרְאֶה — *a woman beautiful of appearance*. The phrase is a **stock formula** in biblical narrative for the dangerously attractive female figure. // **The formula's recurrences across the Hebrew Bible** track the cases where a woman's beauty becomes consequential: **Rebekah** at Gen 26:7 (*tovat mar'eh*, 'good of appearance' — applied within the wife-sister type-scene's second instance); **Rachel** at Gen 29:17 (*yefat to'ar v'yefat mar'eh*, the doubled form 'beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance' — Jacob's love at first sight); **Joseph** at Gen 39:6 (*yefeh to'ar v'yefeh mar'eh*, the same doubled form in masculine — making Joseph one of only two men in the Hebrew Bible explicitly described with the beauty-formula; the other is David at 1 Sam 16:12); **Abigail** at 1 Sam 25:3 (*tovat sekhel v'yefat to'ar*, intelligence-and-beauty); **Tamar** daughter of Absalom at 2 Sam 14:27 (*ishah yefat mar'eh*); **Bathsheba** at 2 Sam 11:2 (*tovat mar'eh me'od* — the seeing-from-the-roof scene); **Abishag** the Shunammite at 1 Kgs 1:3–4 (*na'arah yafah ... yafah ad-me'od*); **Vashti** at Esther 1:11 (*tovat mar'eh*); **Esther** at Esth 2:7 (*yefat to'ar v'tovat mar'eh*). // The formula functions in the narrative as a **plot-trigger**: it signals that the woman's beauty is about to drive consequential events. Sarai's beauty here will drive the Pharaoh-episode; Rebekah's at 26:7 will drive the Abimelech-episode; Rachel's will drive Jacob's fourteen years of labor; Bathsheba's will drive the David-Uriah crisis; Esther's will drive the deliverance of the diaspora. The Hebrew Bible's storytelling reserves the beauty-formula for cases where beauty becomes a vector of narrative force. // The WoH translation preserves the formulaic structure *a woman beautiful of appearance* — over ASV's 'a fair woman to look upon' (archaic) and modern 'a beautiful woman' (which dissolves the formula). The intratextual signal is preserved.

paragraphs.text: וְהָיָ֗ה כִּֽי־יִרְא֤וּ אֹתָךְ֙ הַמִּצְרִ֔ים וְאָמְר֖וּ אִשְׁתּ֣וֹ זֹ֑את וְהָרְג֥וּ אֹתִ֖י וְאֹתָ֥ךְ יְחַיּֽוּ׃

i18n.en: And it shall come to pass that when the Mitsrim see you, they will say, 'This is his wife,' and they will kill me and let you live.

paragraphs.text: אִמְרִי־נָ֖א אֲחֹ֣תִי אָ֑תְּ לְמַ֙עַן֙ יִֽיטַב־לִ֣י בַעֲבוּרֵ֔ךְ וְחָיְתָ֥ה נַפְשִׁ֖י בִּגְלָלֵֽךְ׃

i18n.en: Say, please, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me on your account, and my soul shall live because of you.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter's most ethically debated verse.** *Imri-na achoti at* — *say, please, that you are my sister*. The strategy: have Sarai claim to be Abram's sister rather than his wife, so that a Pharaonic appropriation of her (which Abram is treating as inevitable given her beauty) will not require killing the husband. // **Three readings of Abram's strategy circulate.** // **(a) The morally-compromised reading** (Speiser, 1964; Sarna, JPS, 1989; Westermann, 1985; Hamilton, NICOT, 1990; Alter, 2004 — the modern critical mainstream). Abram is lying to save his own life by exposing Sarai to sexual appropriation. The story is included in the patriarchal cycle precisely because it is morally ambiguous — the patriarchs of Genesis are not idealized; the narrative records their lapses (Abram and Hagar in ch 16; Jacob's deception of Isaac in 27; Judah and Tamar in 38; Joseph's brothers' fratricidal plot in 37). The verse-form's *na* (politeness particle) and *l'ma'an yitav-li* (*so that it may go well with me*) make Abram's self-interest explicit. The Pharaoh-episode that follows will deliver an implicit narrative judgment: Pharaoh rebukes Abram in v 18 (*what is this you have done to me?*) for the deception, and YHWH afflicts Pharaoh's house only because of what Abram has set in motion. // **(b) The apologetic-rabbinic reading** (Genesis Rabbah 41:2; the targumim; Rashi). Abram's claim is technically true — Sarai is Abram's half-sister (per Gen 20:12, where Abraham tells Abimelech *she is indeed my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother*). The strategy is a *partial truth* deployed under duress, not a full lie. On this reading Abram's deception is mitigated. // **(c) The defensive-tactical reading** (some modern apologetic commentators; less common in critical scholarship). Abram is acting within the constraints of a foreign court system in which marriage protections did not extend to traveling foreigners. The sister-designation activates kinship-negotiation protocols that would not have applied to a foreign couple presented as married, where the husband would simply be removed. On this reading the strategy is risky but pragmatic, and the moral weight falls on the foreign system that creates the constraint. // **The Sarai-as-half-sister claim of 20:12 is itself complicated** — the verse appears only in the second wife-sister episode and may be apologetic redactional material aimed at exactly the problem the chapter creates. Critical scholarship is divided on whether 20:12 should be read as authentic Abrahamic genealogy or as later harmonization. // The chapter at 12:13 does not editorialize on the strategy. The verbs *yitav-li* (it may go well with me) and *chaytah nafshi* (my soul shall live) are stated baldly in Abram's voice. The narrative judgment, such as it is, will come through Pharaoh's rebuke in v 18 and through the parallel re-tellings at chs 20 and 26 — each of which the redactor chose to preserve.

paragraphs.text: וַיְהִ֕י כְּב֥וֹא אַבְרָ֖ם מִצְרָ֑יְמָה וַיִּרְא֤וּ הַמִּצְרִים֙ אֶת־הָ֣אִשָּׁ֔ה כִּֽי־יָפָ֥ה הִ֖וא מְאֹֽד׃

i18n.en: When Abram entered Mitsrayim, the Mitsrim saw the woman, that she was very beautiful.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּרְא֤וּ אֹתָהּ֙ שָׂרֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔ה וַיְהַֽלְל֥וּ אֹתָ֖הּ אֶל־פַּרְעֹ֑ה וַתֻּקַּ֥ח הָאִשָּׁ֖ה בֵּ֥ית פַּרְעֹֽה׃

i18n.en: The officers of Pharaoh saw her and praised her to Pharaoh, and the woman was taken into the house of Pharaoh.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Sarei Par'oh*** — שָׂרֵי פַרְעֹה — *the officers of Pharaoh* (plural of *sar*, prince / official / commander). The Pharaonic court structure assumed by the narrative is familiar from the Joseph cycle (chs 39–41) and the Exodus (Ex 1:11): a hierarchy of *sarim* who serve the king and conduct his affairs of state. The verse moves with brisk procedural language — the officers *see*, then *praise*, then the woman *is taken*. The grammatical passive *vatuqqach* (was taken) keeps the agency diffuse: Sarai is taken into the royal household without the verse naming who exactly does the taking, in keeping with the court-procedural register.

paragraphs.text: וּלְאַבְרָ֥ם הֵיטִ֖יב בַּעֲבוּרָ֑הּ וַֽיְהִי־ל֤וֹ צֹאן־וּבָקָר֙ וַחֲמֹרִ֔ים וַעֲבָדִים֙ וּשְׁפָחֹ֔ת וַאֲתֹנֹ֖ת וּגְמַלִּֽים׃

i18n.en: And he treated Abram well on her account; and he had sheep and cattle and male donkeys and male slaves and female slaves and female donkeys and camels.

paragraphs.commentary: **The camels at the end of the gift-list are the patriarchal narratives' most-cited anachronism.** The seven-item inventory is otherwise plausible for second-millennium-BCE Levantine pastoralism: *tzon* (sheep / small cattle), *baqar* (cattle / oxen), *chamorim* (male donkeys), *avadim* (male slaves), *shfachot* (female slaves), *atonot* (female donkeys), *g'mallim* (camels). The first six fit the Bronze Age economy without controversy. The seventh does not. // **The archaeological consensus on camel domestication in the southern Levant** places the appearance of the domesticated camel as a working pack animal between roughly 1000 and 900 BCE — the early Iron Age, well into the period of the Israelite monarchy. The decisive recent study is **Sapir-Hen and Ben-Yosef, 'The Introduction of Domestic Camels to the Southern Levant: Evidence from the Aravah Valley', *Tel Aviv* 40 (2013): 277–285** — a stratigraphic analysis of camel bones in the Aravah copper-mining sites that pins the introduction to the late tenth century BCE. Earlier reviews of the evidence (Köhler-Rollefson, 'Camels and Camel Pastoralism in Arabia', *Biblical Archaeologist* 56/4, 1993) reached the same conclusion from different evidence. Finkelstein and Silberman, *The Bible Unearthed* (2001), made the Iron Age dating widely known in popular scholarship. // **The patriarchal narratives are conventionally placed in the Middle Bronze Age** (ca. 2000–1500 BCE) or, on some chronologies, the Late Bronze Age (ca. 1500–1200 BCE). Both placements are centuries earlier than the documented arrival of the domesticated camel as a Levantine working animal. The camels at Gen 12:16 (and at 24:10–11, 30:43, 31:17, 32:7, 37:25) are therefore widely read as **redactional anachronism** — markers of the post-monarchic period in which the narratives reached final form, projected backward onto an earlier setting. // **The standard scholarly inference** is that the patriarchal narratives were composed or finalized in a period when camel pastoralism was familiar (the late monarchic or post-exilic redactor would have known camels as part of the standard pastoral inventory) and the camel was projected backward as a generic luxury-trade-animal. The four wife-sister episodes' mentions of camels (here at 12:16; at 24:10–11 — the most prominent, with ten camels in Abraham's servant's mission to Aram-Naharaim; at 30:43; at 37:25) are concentrated in J/E material, consistent with later compositional dating. // The WoH translation renders the inventory item straight as 'camels' — the editorial question is for commentary, not for translation. The text-as-received names camels; the historical-critical question is when the text-as-received reached this form, and what that implies about its compositional dating.

paragraphs.text: וַיְנַגַּ֨ע יְהוָ֧ה ׀ אֶת־פַּרְעֹ֛ה נְגָעִ֥ים גְּדֹלִ֖ים וְאֶת־בֵּית֑וֹ עַל־דְּבַ֥ר שָׂרַ֖י אֵ֥שֶׁת אַבְרָֽם׃

i18n.en: YHWH afflicted Pharaoh and his house with great plagues on account of Sarai, the wife of Abram.

paragraphs.commentary: **The first plague-on-a-Pharaoh in the Hebrew Bible, and the verse most often cited in scholarship on Genesis 12 as proto-Exodus typology.** // *Vaynagga YHWH et-Par'oh n'ga'im g'dolim* — *YHWH afflicted Pharaoh with great plagues*. The verb *naga* (n-g-' qal) means *touch, strike, afflict, smite*. The cognate noun *nega* (plague, blow, stroke, affliction-mark) is the technical Hebrew term for divinely-sent affliction across the Pentateuch. Leviticus 13–14 uses *nega* extensively for the ritual-impurity category of skin-disease (the so-called *tzara'at* of 'leprosy'). Deuteronomy 24:8 uses *nega ha-tzara'at* in the same sense. The root carries a specifically *cultic-juridical* connotation: the plague is not natural illness but divinely-imposed mark. // **The chapter's typological link to the Exodus is structurally precise.** The Exodus narrative uses the same root *naga / nega* for the divine plagues against Egypt: most decisively at **Exodus 11:1**, in YHWH's announcement of the tenth plague to Moses: *od nega echad avi al-Par'oh v'al-Mitsrayim* — *one more plague (nega) I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Mitsrayim*. The same noun, the same construction with *al* (upon), the same subject (YHWH), the same object (Pharaoh and Mitsrayim). The verbal echo across the two passages is one of the patriarchal corpus's most discussed structural parallels. // **The Abram-Pharaoh / Moses-Pharaoh parallel structure** can be tabulated cleanly: a famine drives Israel down to Mitsrayim → Pharaoh oppresses (here by taking Sarai; in Exodus by enslavement) → YHWH afflicts Pharaoh with plagues (n'ga'im g'dolim / n'ga'im) → Pharaoh summons the Hebrew patriarch / prophet (v 18 here; Exod 12:31 there) → Pharaoh expels the Hebrews (v 20 here; Exod 12:33 there) → the Hebrews depart with great substance (vv 16, 20 — the gift-list; Exod 12:35–36 — the spoiling of the Egyptians). The structural parallel is extensive enough that critical scholarship (Garbini, *History and Ideology in Ancient Israel*, 1988; Crüsemann; Sarna's JPS commentary on Genesis 12) treats Gen 12:10–20 as a **deliberate prefiguration** of the Exodus, composed or redacted in light of the later narrative. // **The two readings of the parallel** in critical scholarship are: (a) **typological redaction** — Gen 12:10–20 was composed late, modeled on the Exodus narrative, and inserted into the Abrahamic cycle to establish Abram as proto-Moses and the patriarchal descent-and-return as proto-Exodus; (b) **convergent type-scene** — both narratives draw on a common Mesopotamian or Egyptian topos of the foreign-court appropriation-and-deliverance, with no necessary direction of dependence. Most modern critical scholars (Westermann, Sarna, Alter) favor (a). // The verse's *al-d'var Sarai eshet Avram* (*on account of Sarai the wife of Abram*) makes the causal link explicit: the plagues are YHWH's response specifically to the Pharaonic appropriation of Sarai. The chapter is silent about what made the link visible to Pharaoh — the next verse will reveal that Pharaoh somehow knows the cause.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֤א פַרְעֹה֙ לְאַבְרָ֔ם וַיֹּ֕אמֶר מַה־זֹּ֖את עָשִׂ֣יתָ לִּ֑י לָ֚מָּה לֹא־הִגַּ֣דְתָּ לִּ֔י כִּ֥י אִשְׁתְּךָ֖ הִֽוא׃

i18n.en: Pharaoh called Abram and said, "What is this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that she is your wife?

paragraphs.commentary: **Pharaoh's rebuke delivers the chapter's implicit moral judgment on Abram's strategy.** *Mah-zot asita li* — *what is this you have done to me?* — uses the same construction (*mah-zot asita*) that YHWH addressed to Eve at Gen 3:13 (*mah-zot asit*, 'what is this you have done?'). The rebuke-formula is consistent across the corpus: the more powerful party confronts the less powerful with the consequences of a hidden act. Here the formula's polarity is striking — *Pharaoh* is addressing *Abram* in the register that elsewhere belongs to *YHWH* addressing humans. The chapter is staging a foreign king as the agent of moral truth-telling against the patriarch. The narrative judgment lands on Abram from the unexpected direction. // *Lamah lo higgad'ta li ki ishtekha hi* — *why did you not tell me that she is your wife?* — assumes a moral framework in which appropriating another man's wife is wrong and Abram's concealment is culpable. Pharaoh is invoking a standard the verse takes for granted, without exposition. The rebuke is brief and pointed.

paragraphs.text: לָמָ֤ה אָמַ֙רְתָּ֙ אֲחֹ֣תִי הִ֔וא וָאֶקַּ֥ח אֹתָ֛הּ לִ֖י לְאִשָּׁ֑ה וְעַתָּ֕ה הִנֵּ֥ה אִשְׁתְּךָ֖ קַ֥ח וָלֵֽךְ׃

i18n.en: Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her for myself as a wife? Now then, here is your wife — take her and go.

paragraphs.text: וַיְצַ֥ו עָלָ֛יו פַּרְעֹ֖ה אֲנָשִׁ֑ים וַֽיְשַׁלְּח֥וּ אֹת֛וֹ וְאֶת־אִשְׁתּ֖וֹ וְאֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־לֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Pharaoh commanded men concerning him, and they sent him away with his wife and all that he had.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter closes with the verb that will close the Exodus.** *Vay'shal'chu oto* — *and they sent him away*. // The verb *shalach* in the piel stem (*shillach*) is the Hebrew Bible's standard term for **expulsion / sending-out / dismissal** of persons. The piel intensifies the qal *shalach* (send) toward forced removal: not merely *send* but *send off, dismiss, expel, set free*. The same piel verb governs the keystone Exodus moments: // **Exodus 6:1** — YHWH's promise to Moses that Pharaoh will send Israel out: *b'yad chazaqah y'shalchem u-v'yad chazaqah y'gar'shem me-artzo* — *with a strong hand he will send them out (y'shalchem), and with a strong hand he will drive them out from his land*. // **Exodus 11:1** — YHWH's announcement of the tenth plague: *acharei khen y'shalach et'khem mi-zeh, k'shalcho kalah garesh y'garesh et'khem mi-zeh* — *after that he will send you out (y'shalach) from here; when he sends you out completely (k'shalcho kalah), he will utterly drive you out from here*. // **Exodus 12:33** — the immediate aftermath of the tenth plague: *vatechezaq Mitsrayim al-ha-am l'maher l'shalcham min ha-aretz* — *the Mitsrim were urgent upon the people, to send them out (l'shalcham) from the land in haste*. // The verbal link is exact. **The Abram-expulsion of 12:20 is verbally identical to the Israel-expulsion of Exod 12:33** — the same piel of *sh-l-ch*, the same context of Pharaonic dismissal under divine pressure, the same outcome of departure with great substance. The chapter is verbally closing its proto-Exodus structure with the verb that will verbally open the Exodus's final scene. // The structural parallel discussed in scholarship (Sarna, JPS, 1989; Garbini; Crüsemann; the wider Pentateuchal-criticism literature) extends to the detail of *vay'shal'chu oto v'et-ishto v'et-kol-asher-lo* (sent him with his wife and all that he had), which closely parallels the Exodus departure-of-Israel-with-spoils. The chapter ends with Abram-and-household leaving Mitsrayim wealthier than they arrived, escorted out under royal command — the prefiguration of what Israel will do at the Exodus.
